what_this_is.heading: What this is
what_this_is.p1: The Forge runs local models on this box's own GPU and routes to remote providers through the same interface, so both look the same to whatever's asking for a completion.
what_this_is.p2: Console is the operational view: what's loaded right now, in four load bays (A1–A4), plus provider and service health. Dashboard covers cost and power across three tabs (Overview, Cost, Resources). Models is the full catalog: every model, its variants, and the local configs and remote offerings that serve them. Scheduling covers the on-demand loader's tunables and reservations. Settings is a left-sidebar shell grouped by what it changes: General; Money (Providers, Billing); Traffic (Routing); Workload (Scheduling, Monitoring, smith); Catalog (the catalog editor, Benchmarks & Profiling); Access (Security); and Danger Zone.
what_this_is.p3: A model is the underlying weights (one entry per model on the Models page). A variant is a specific derivation of it (a quant, a fine-tune). A config is a concrete local launch recipe for a variant (engine build, context length, backend, cache type, every launch flag of its engine: llama.cpp, Radiance or vLLM) and what actually gets loaded into a bay. An offering is the remote equivalent: a model served by a specific provider at a specific price.

load_bays.heading: Load bays
load_bays.p1: Four bays, A1–A4. Console shows only the bays that are actually in use (loaded, loading, unloading, or reserved) plus the first free one, so an idle box shows just A1 with a "+ Load model" button rather than four empty slots. The scheduler places a load on whichever bay is free, never a fixed one, so nothing outside this app should ever assume a model lives on a specific bay.
load_bays.p2: Loading a model can be refused. The most common reason is the fit check: the scheduler won't load something it doesn't have enough free memory (VRAM/GTT) for, given what's already loaded in the other bays. If a load is refused, check what else is running before assuming something is broken.

ejecting.heading: Ejecting
ejecting.p1: Eject frees a bay immediately. Nothing is unloaded on a timer: an idle model stays loaded until you eject it or another request needs its memory. The idle window (Scheduling → Scheduler tunables) is how long a model must have been unused before the scheduler may evict it for that other request.

on_demand.heading: On-demand loading
on_demand.p1: Nothing needs to be manually loaded before use: the scheduler loads a model on first request, and evicts an idle one only when another request needs the room. The Scheduling page sets the tunables: how long a model must be idle before it may be evicted, a small-job token threshold, and a priority-jump cap that lets a small, fast request cut ahead of a long-running one already queued.

reservations.heading: Reservations
reservations.p1: A reservation guarantees a bay for a model at (or from) a specific time, useful for anything that can't tolerate a cold-load delay, including scheduled ComfyUI jobs. The Scheduling page shows upcoming reservations and lets you cancel one.

adding_hf.heading: Adding a model from HuggingFace
adding_hf.p1: Models → Add Model searches HuggingFace directly, ranks a repo's real GGUF files against this host's live memory budget, and runs pre-flight checks (disk headroom, which backend the file needs, an existing-file conflict) before you commit to anything.
adding_hf.p2: Clicking Download starts a real, resumable transfer: pause and resume pick up from where they left off rather than restarting, and a repo split into shards (…-00001-of-00003.gguf and friends) downloads as one job. Progress, speed, and ETA show live in the Downloads list at the top of that tab.
adding_hf.p3: Once verified, the model registers itself into the catalog automatically: a new Model, Variant, Artifact, and Config, with sensible defaults (--parallel 1, the model's own trained context, the right backend for its size). The new Config lands unverified and hidden on purpose: it won't appear in the dashboard switcher until you open it and promote it, the same review step every other catalog entry goes through.
adding_hf.p4: Gated repos (license click-through models like Gemma or Llama) need a HuggingFace access token first; set one in Settings → Security. A repo you have a specific artifact for already can also be pointed at an existing config instead of registering a new one, by supplying that config's name when starting the download via the API or through smith.

editing.heading: Editing in place
editing.p1: Opening a config or model card gives you an expanded detail view; its Edit button opens a premium editor in the same place, no jump to a different tab. Every field is available, including the structural ones (backend, weight artifact, mmproj).

flag_picker.heading: The flag picker
flag_picker.p1: Launch flags are tap-to-select rather than freeform text, with an explanation of what each one does, and for two llama.cpp flags, an inline hazard warning:
flag_picker.p2: --parallel above 1 splits the config's own context across that many slots rather than multiplying it, so a model configured for 128K context with --parallel 2 actually serves 64K per request. Anything meant to serve one long conversation at its full configured context needs --parallel 1.
flag_picker.p3: --ctx-checkpoints set to a non-zero value on certain model architectures can hit an upstream llama.cpp hang bug. The picker warns inline rather than silently letting it through; if you're unsure whether a specific model is affected, leave it at 0.
flag_picker.p4: Anything not in the curated list still works: it falls into an Advanced section as a raw flag/value pair, or the freeform escape hatch. Every save can carry an optional "why this change" note, visible afterward in the config or model's own change history.

notes.heading: Notes
notes.p1: Below Key features on a model or config's detail view, Notes is a place for operator judgment that isn't a curated benchmark or a change-history entry: "tends to truncate long outputs," "needs the reasoning-fix build," anything the next person looking at this model should know. Admins can add, edit, and delete inline; everyone can read.

benchmarks.heading: Benchmarks & Profiling
benchmarks.p1: Settings → Benchmarks & Profiling groups curated performance/capability scores by config: a config's own benchmarks first, then what it inherits from its variant and model (a scope chip on each row always names which one it actually came from), next to that config's own measured profile if one exists. Profiling is the destructive part: "Profile…" evicts whatever else is loaded to measure one config alone: memory footprint and prefill/decode throughput at four context depths (empty, 25%, 50%, ~full), and always shows exactly which bays will be evicted before you confirm.

speech_services.heading: Speech services
speech_services.p1: Settings → Voice & Speech's Speech services card starts and stops STT, Embedding, and Aligner independently. A blank/"Not configured" chip means the service genuinely has no dedicated resident unit on this host, not a loading glitch.

voice_engines.heading: Speech engines
voice_engines.p1: Settings → Voice & Speech starts with What works: preset voices, voice cloning and voice design, each with what it is missing. An engine whose files are already on the server is set up with one button (admin), which adds a dedicated slot if one is needed and makes the engine the default for its kind of voice if there is none. + Add engine lists every engine the server can set up, with the install command for the ones it can build. forge speech status, recipes and register do the same from a terminal.

listing_voices.heading: Listing voices
listing_voices.p1: List all voices, on the Voices card, shows every voice and the engine that makes it. Voices are made in Voice Studio (record, clone or describe), not on this page.

measured_vs_estimated.heading: What's measured vs. estimated
measured_vs_estimated.p1: Dashboard → Overview shows the box's real, measured electricity draw (a live power sensor), not an estimate. Dashboard → Cost separates that real electricity cost from virtual spend (what local inference would have cost at a comparable API's prices, a counterfactual, not a bill) and real API spend (what remote-provider requests through a0 actually cost, tracked from each response's own usage data). These are three different numbers and are deliberately never summed into one "total cost": electricity and virtual spend are two different estimates of the same local draw, not additive costs.

compressor_savings.heading: The prompt compressor (retired)
compressor_savings.p1: Forge no longer compresses or rewrites request context: editing earlier messages throws away the model's cached prefix, so every turn would be processed again. Savings figures that still appear on the Dashboard are history from before the compressor was retired. To keep context small, look at who is creating it (the context creation panel on the Dashboard).

a0_router.heading: The a0 router
a0_router.p1: a0 is an OpenAI-compatible endpoint that fronts both local load bays and remote providers, so an external agent talks to one address regardless of where a given model actually runs. It's the integration point for anything outside this app: OpenCode, LibreChat, or a custom client.

getting_a_key.heading: Getting a key
getting_a_key.p1: Settings → Security → API keys mints a bearer key for a machine consumer; pick kind router for an a0 consumer (OpenCode, LibreChat, a custom client) and give it a name. The token is shown once, at creation time; copy it immediately, since the server never echoes it back afterward. Revoke a key from the same list. Use the model names shown on the Models page as the wire model name in requests.

mcp.heading: MCP
mcp.p1: A separate MCP server exposes scheduler control (status, load, evict) as tools for an agent that needs to manage its own inference resources rather than just call them. Mint an MCP-kind key the same way, from Settings → Security → API keys, kind mcp.

providers.heading: Providers
providers.p1: Settings → Providers links a remote provider (a curated preset prefills the endpoint, billing API, and currency where one exists) and stores its API key write-only, once saved, the key is never echoed back by the server, only a masked form. A provider can be renamed in place, and its page shows the actual models it serves (built from real offerings, not a static count) rather than just a chip.

assurance.heading: Assurance levels & step-up
assurance.p1: Sensitive actions (provider keys, security settings, load/unload, reservations) require a minimum assurance level. Network identity and a valid password get you the base level; a step-up prompt (password, TOTP, or a passkey) raises it temporarily when an action needs more than you currently have, and expires after the configured step-up TTL.

totp.heading: TOTP, passkeys, recovery codes
totp.p1: Settings → Security lets you enroll a TOTP authenticator app, register a WebAuthn passkey (hardware key or biometric, the strongest factor), and generate recovery codes for account recovery if you lose access to both. Recovery codes are shown once at generation time; store them somewhere safe.
